verses.context: The chapter opens right after 10:33-34, where God lops the lofty trees of Assyria's forest and Lebanon falls. Against that crash comes a single green shoot from a stump. The royal hope survives the felling of David's house, but it starts again as small as a sprout, and verses 2 to 5 will describe the king who grows from it.
verses.grammar: Choter is a twig or fresh shoot, and geza is the stump left after a tree is cut down (the word appears elsewhere only in 40:24 and Job 14:8). The stump is Jesse's, not David's: the promise goes back behind the failed kings to the family of Bethlehem before David was anointed, as if God were starting the dynasty over. The parallel line names netser, a green sprout from the roots. The verbs move from veyatsa, ‘and it will come out’ (a consecutive perfect pointing to the future), to yifreh, "will bear fruit".
verses.text: The Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate have ‘will rise up’ or ‘will grow’ instead of ‘will bear fruit’, as if reading yifrach, ‘will sprout’, for yifreh; the two differ by one letter, and many modern scholars prefer the sprouting sense as a better parallel to ‘will come out’. The Aramaic Targum renders the verse explicitly of the Messiah: a king will come forth from the sons of Jesse, and the Messiah will be anointed from his sons' sons.
verses.history: Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a commentary on Isaiah from Qumran (4Q161, the Isaiah Pesher A) interprets this passage of the Branch of David who will arise at the end of days, and another text (4Q285) reads 10:34 to 11:1 of the Branch of David defeating the Kittim, the scrolls' name for the final enemy. In Christian art the verse produced the Tree of Jesse, a genealogy of Christ growing from the sleeping Jesse, as in the twelfth century window of Chartres Cathedral, and the German carol Es ist ein Ros entsprungen (‘Lo, how a rose e'er blooming’) sings the same shoot.

theology.note: The Messiah arises from a stump, not a flourishing tree. The verse teaches that God's king will come when David's house looks finished, which the Gospels answer by setting Jesus' birth among poor descendants of David in an occupied land (Luke 2:4-7). The humble origin is part of the promise, not an embarrassment to it.

verses.context: The shoot is equipped by the Spirit of the LORD, which rests on him with three pairs of gifts: wisdom and understanding for the mind, counsel and might for decision and action, knowledge and the fear of the LORD for his relation to God. This inner equipment is the ground for the just rule described in verses 3 to 5.
verses.grammar: Venachah, "will rest", is the verb nuach, ‘to settle, come to rest’. It describes the spirit resting on the seventy elders (Numbers 11:25-26) and the spirit of Elijah resting on Elisha (2 Kings 2:15): the Spirit is not a momentary visitation, as with the judges, but a settled presence. Ruach appears four times in the verse, the Spirit of the LORD followed by three construct chains, each ‘spirit of’ two qualities. The pairs are chokhmah and binah, practical wisdom and discernment; etsah and gevurah, counsel and might, the same pair as in the throne name ‘Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God’ (9:6); and daat and yirat YHWH, knowledge of and reverence for the LORD.
verses.text: The Septuagint renders the last pair as ‘knowledge and piety’ (eusebeia) and then translates the phrase ‘fear of the LORD’ at the start of verse 3 as a further gift, the spirit of the fear of God. The Latin followed it, yielding seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. This became the medieval and Catholic teaching on the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, developed by Thomas Aquinas and still taught in the Catechism of the Catholic Church. The Hebrew has six qualities in three pairs, with the fear of the LORD repeated in verse 3.

theology.note: The Messiah is the Spirit-bearer. The Gospels show the Spirit descending and remaining on Jesus at his baptism (John 1:32-33), and in Nazareth Jesus reads the related promise of Isaiah 61:1 as fulfilled in himself. Christian theology has drawn from this verse that the Son's human life was lived in dependence on the Spirit.
Wisdom here is a gift, not an achievement, and it is inseparable from the fear of the LORD, the beginning of wisdom in Proverbs 1:7. The king's competence rests on his reverence.

verses.context: The Spirit's gifts show in how the king judges. His delight is in the fear of the LORD, and he will not rule by appearances or rumor. Verse 4 then states the positive: he judges by righteousness, especially for the poor.
verses.grammar: Vaharicho beyirat YHWH, "He will delight in the fear of the LORD", is literally ‘his smelling will be in the fear of the LORD’. Heriach is a Hiphil of the root ruach, the same root as ‘spirit’ in verse 2, and it means to smell or savor. It is the verb used when God smells the pleasing aroma of Noah's sacrifice (Genesis 8:21) and refuses to smell Israel's festivals (Amos 5:21). The wordplay is deliberate: the one on whom the ruach rests will have a nose for the fear of God. Lemareh einav, ‘by the sight of his eyes’, and lemishma oznav, ‘by the hearing of his ears’, name the two ways ordinary judges are misled. Yokhiach, "decide", is a Hiphil of yakach, ‘to set right, arbitrate’.

theology.note: Judging by appearance is how the powerful win: the rich look credible and the poor do not. A king who sees past appearances, as God does when he looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7), is the only kind of judge the poor can trust. John 7:24 has Jesus warn against judging by appearance.

verses.context: The king's justice favors the poor and the humble, and his power against the wicked lies in his word. There is no army in the verse: the rod he strikes with is the rod of his mouth, and the breath of his lips is enough to end the wicked.
verses.grammar: Dallim, "the poor", are the weak and impoverished; anvei-arets, "the lowly of the earth", are the afflicted and humble, a word close to the anvah of Psalm 45:4. Bemishor, "with equity", is literally ‘with levelness’, a judgment that does not tilt. The verse then turns to the wicked with two instruments: beshevet piv, ‘with the rod of his mouth’, and beruach sefatav, ‘with the breath (ruach) of his lips’, the third meaning of ruach in the passage after Spirit and smell. Yamit, "He will slay", is a Hiphil of mut, ‘to cause to die’.
verses.text: "He will strike the earth" reads erets, ‘earth’, which many scholars think should be arits, ‘the ruthless one’, a difference of one letter that would give a closer parallel to ‘the wicked’ in the next line. The ancient versions support erets. The Septuagint renders ‘the word of his mouth’ and ‘the ungodly’, wording that shapes the New Testament's echo.
verses.history: The verse became a standard description of the Messiah in Jewish writings around the time of Jesus. The Psalms of Solomon (17, first century BC) pray for a son of David who will destroy lawless nations with the word of his mouth. The Rule of the Blessings from Qumran (1QSb 5) blesses the future Prince of the Congregation with the language of this verse: to strike the peoples with the might of his mouth and to slay the wicked with the breath of his lips.

theology.note: The Messiah's judgment is carried out by his word. The New Testament keeps the image: the Lord Jesus will overthrow the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8), and the rider of Revelation 19:15 strikes the nations with a sword from his mouth.

nt.note: Paul says the lawless one will be revealed and the Lord Jesus will slay him ‘with the breath of his mouth’. The phrase is close to the Septuagint of this verse (‘he will destroy the ungodly with breath through his lips’), and Paul applies Isaiah's picture of the Davidic king's judgment directly to the returning Jesus. Revelation 19:15 and 19:21 develop the same image into the sharp sword coming from the rider's mouth.

verses.context: The king's clothing is his character. Righteousness and faithfulness are the belt he fastens to be ready for action. The description of the king closes here, and the poem turns in verse 6 to the peace of his realm.
verses.grammar: The verse repeats ezor, "belt", in both lines: ezor motnav, ‘the belt of his hips’, and ezor chalatsav, ‘the belt of his loins’. To gird the loins was to tuck up a robe for work, travel, or battle (1 Kings 18:46). Tsedeq, "Righteousness", and haemunah, "faithfulness", the reliability that comes from the root aman (7:9), are what hold him together and make him ready.

theology.note: The king's rule is only as good as his character, and the verse makes righteousness and faithfulness the things that hold him together. Isaiah's kingdom is never merely a transfer of power to Israel; it is the reign of a king whose own integrity makes justice possible for everyone under him.

Paul takes up this image and the related one of 59:17 for believers: stand firm with the belt of truth around your waist and the breastplate of righteousness (Ephesians 6:14). The king's own equipment becomes the armor of those who belong to him.

verses.context: The king's reign reaches the animal world. Predators and prey live together: wolf and lamb, leopard and young goat, calf and lion, cow and bear. A small child leads them, and the lion eats straw like the ox. The pairs are chosen so that each predator lies down with its natural victim.
verses.grammar: Vegar, "will live", is from gur, ‘to sojourn as a guest’, the verb for a resident alien living under another's protection: the wolf becomes the lamb's guest. Yirbats, "will lie down", is the word for a flock resting (Psalm 23:2). Naar qaton, ‘a little boy’, noheg bam, ‘leading them’, uses the ordinary verb for driving a flock. Verse 7 turns the diet around: the lion eats teven, chopped straw, like the ox.
verses.text: In verse 6 ‘and the fatling’ (umeri) is read by the Septuagint as a verb, ‘and (they) will graze together’, as if the Hebrew were yimreu. Several modern translations follow it. Isaiah 65:25 reprises the scene more briefly: the wolf and the lamb will feed together.
verses.history: Ancient literature outside Israel also dreamed of a golden age of peace among animals. The Roman poet Virgil's Fourth Eclogue (about 40 BC) imagines a coming child in whose age herds will not fear great lions and the serpent will die. Isaiah's vision differs in its source: the peace flows from the Spirit-filled king and the knowledge of the LORD (verse 9), not from the turning of the ages. The American Quaker painter Edward Hicks painted dozens of versions of this passage in the nineteenth century as The Peaceable Kingdom.

theology.note: The Messiah's peace extends to creation itself. Whether read literally or as a picture of nations at peace (the chapter note sets out both), the passage refuses a salvation that concerns souls alone. Paul speaks of the whole creation waiting to be set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:19-21).

verses.context: The most vulnerable of all, a nursing infant and a just-weaned toddler, play at the holes of snakes unharmed. Verse 9 gives the reason: on God's holy mountain nothing harms or destroys, because the earth is as full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is of water. This is the hinge of the chapter, where the king's realm becomes the whole earth.
verses.grammar: Yoneq, "infant", is a nursing baby and gamul, "toddler", a weaned child, perhaps two or three years old. Peten, "cobra", and tsifoni, "viper", are the most feared snakes of the region. Verse 9's verbs, yareu and yashchitu, ‘they will do harm’ and ‘they will destroy’, are Hiphil imperfects with no stated subject, so they cover both the animals of verses 6 to 8 and the human violence behind them. The reason is introduced by ki, ‘for’: malah haarets deah et-YHWH, ‘the earth will be full of knowledge of the LORD’. Deah is knowing in the full biblical sense, not information but acquaintance and allegiance.

theology.note: The child's hand at the serpent's den quietly reverses the enmity between the serpent and the woman's offspring in Genesis 3:15. The link is thematic rather than verbal, but it fits Isaiah's picture of a world where the curse no longer rules.

The final state of the world is defined by knowledge of God filling everything. Habakkuk 2:14 repeats the line with ‘the knowledge of the glory of the LORD’. The Bible's hope is not only for peace but for God known everywhere, which is why the peace is lasting.

verses.context: The first ‘on that day’ oracle. The Root of Jesse stands as a banner for the peoples, the nations seek him, and his resting place is glory. The king of verses 1 to 5 becomes the rallying point of the world, and verses 11 and 12 will show him gathering Israel's exiles as well.
verses.grammar: The shoot of verse 1 is now shoresh Yishai, "the Root of Jesse": the one who sprang from the root is himself called the root. Omed lenes amim, ‘standing as a banner of peoples’, uses a participle for a fixed position; a nes was a signal pole raised on a hill to rally troops or travelers (5:26, 18:3). Elav goyim yidroshu, ‘to him the nations will seek’, puts ‘to him’ first for emphasis and uses darash, the verb for seeking God at a sanctuary or through a prophet. Menuchato, "His dwelling" or ‘his resting place’, is the word for the ark's resting place in Psalm 132:8 and 14, and kavod, "glorious", is the glory of God's presence.

theology.note: The nations come seeking the king of Israel, not by conquest but because he is lifted up as a sign. The verse is one of the Old Testament's clearest promises that the Messiah belongs to the Gentiles too. Jesus uses the image of being lifted up to draw all people to himself (John 12:32).

nt.note: Paul closes a chain of four Old Testament quotations about Gentiles praising God (Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1, and this verse) with Isaiah 11:10, quoted from the Septuagint: there will be the root of Jesse, the one who rises to rule the nations, and in him the nations will hope. The Greek differs from the Hebrew in two ways Paul makes use of: ‘stands as a banner’ becomes ‘the one who rises (anistamenos) to rule’, a verb Paul's readers would hear as resurrection, and ‘seek him’ becomes ‘hope in him’. Paul then prays that the God of hope will fill them (15:13), making Isaiah's verse the climax of his whole argument that Jews and Gentiles are one people glorifying God together.

Revelation calls Jesus the Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Root of David (5:5), and in 22:16 Jesus calls himself the root and the offspring of David. Like Isaiah's shoot that becomes the root, the title makes the Messiah both David's descendant and his source.

verses.context: The second ‘on that day’ oracle. The Lord reaches out his hand a second time to reclaim the remnant of his people from every land where they have been scattered, from Egypt to Babylonia to the Mediterranean coasts. The phrase ‘a second time’ looks back to the exodus as the first.
verses.grammar: Yosif Adonai shenit yado, ‘the Lord will add a second time his hand’, pairs a Hiphil of yasaf, ‘to do again’, with shenit, ‘a second time’. Liqnot, "to recover", is from qanah, ‘to acquire, buy’, the verb of Exodus 15:16, where Israel is the people God has purchased: the return from exile is a second redemption. Sheer ammo asher yishaer, "the remnant of His people", uses the Niphal of shaar, the root of Shear-jashub's name (7:3).
verses.history: Pathros is the Hebrew form of an Egyptian phrase meaning ‘the southern land’, Upper Egypt. Jeremiah 44:1 names Jewish communities there in the early sixth century BC, and the papyri from Elephantine, an island at Egypt's southern border, document a Jewish military colony with its own temple in the fifth century BC. The list thus names real places where Israelites and Judeans lived in dispersion, whether as deportees or refugees.

theology.note: Exile is not God's last word. The same God who scattered his people by Assyria reaches out to gather them, and Isaiah frames the gathering as a new exodus, the theme that dominates chapters 40 to 55.

verses.context: The banner is raised again, now to gather the exiles of Israel and the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. The same signal that draws the nations in verse 10 also brings Israel home.
verses.grammar: The verse uses paired passive participles with a deliberate change of gender: nidchei Yisrael, ‘the banished (men) of Israel’, masculine, and nefutsot Yehudah, ‘the scattered (women) of Judah’, feminine. The pair covers the whole people. Arba kanfot haarets, "the four corners of the earth", is literally ‘the four wings’ or hems of the earth, the edges of the known world (compare Ezekiel 7:2).
verses.history: The language of this verse entered the daily prayer of the synagogue. The tenth blessing of the Amidah, the central prayer said three times a day, asks God to sound the great shofar for freedom, to raise a banner to gather the exiles, and to gather them together from the four corners of the earth.

theology.note: The promise is to Israel and Judah as a people, and Isaiah joins their regathering to the ingathering of the nations in the same act. Christians differ on how that promise is fulfilled: in the church of Jews and Gentiles together, in a future restoration of the Jewish people, or in both, and Romans 11 is the chief New Testament text on which that discussion turns.

verses.context: The regathered people are reunited. The old rivalry between Ephraim in the north and Judah in the south ends, and together they overcome their neighbors, the Philistines to the west and Edom, Moab, and Ammon to the east. The picture restores the united kingdom of David's day.
verses.grammar: Qinat Efrayim, "the jealousy of Ephraim", uses qinah, the same word as the ‘zeal’ of the LORD in 9:7: the destructive jealousy of the tribes gives way to the saving zeal of God. Verse 13 closes with a chiasm, Efrayim lo-yeqanne et-Yehudah viYehudah lo-yatsor et-Efrayim, ‘Ephraim will not envy Judah, and Judah will not harass Ephraim’, the two names crossing in the middle. In verse 14 veafu vekhatef Pelishtim, "They will swoop down on the slopes", is literally ‘they will fly on the shoulder of the Philistines’, a bird of prey diving on the foothills (katef, ‘shoulder’, used for a hill slope).
verses.history: Every nation named in verse 14 was conquered or made tributary by David (2 Samuel 8:1-14): the Philistines, Moab, Edom, and Ammon. The oracle restores the borders and the unity of the Davidic kingdom before its division around 930 BC.

theology.note: The healing of a centuries-old division between brothers is part of the messianic hope. Ezekiel 37:15-22 pictures the two sticks of Judah and Joseph joined into one in God's hand, and Paul describes Christ breaking down the dividing wall of hostility to make one new people (Ephesians 2:14-16).

verses.context: The chapter ends with a new exodus. The LORD strikes the tongue of the Egyptian sea and splits the River into seven streams so that his people can cross in sandals, and he builds a highway for the remnant from Assyria like the road Israel had coming out of Egypt.
verses.grammar: Veheicherim, "will devote to destruction", is the Hiphil of charam, the verb for placing something under the ban. Many scholars read instead heecheriv, ‘will dry up’ (from charav), which differs by one similar letter and fits the parting of waters. Leshon yam-Mitsrayim, ‘the tongue of the Sea of Egypt’, is a gulf or inlet, probably of the Red Sea. "The River" (hannahar) without a name means the Euphrates. Baayam, "scorching", occurs only here and its meaning is a guess from context. Vehidrikh bannealim, ‘he will make them march in sandals’, means the river will be so dry that no one needs to take off his shoes. In verse 16 mesillah, "highway", is a built-up road, the word of 40:3.

theology.note: The return from exile is pictured as the exodus repeated, with the Euphrates playing the part of the Red Sea. Israel's hope is grounded in what God has already done: the one who made a road through the sea will make a road home. Isaiah develops the highway into the Way of Holiness (35:8) and the highway for God himself (40:3).
